params.question: A patient on NTEP treatment has CBNAAT showing rifampicin resistance. What is the most appropriate immediate action at the PHC?

answers.text: Continue the standard HREZ regimen and recheck sputum smear after two months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rifampicin is the backbone of the standard regimen. Once resistance is detected, continuing the same regimen risks failure and further resistance, so this approach is wrong.

answers.text: Refer the patient immediately to a drug-resistant TB centre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rifampicin resistance means the patient needs a DR-TB regimen with a longer and more toxic course. Only a DR-TB centre can start and supervise this, so immediate referral is the correct action.

answers.text: Stop all treatment until culture results return

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Interrupting treatment in TB raises the risk of further drug resistance and loss to follow-up. Treatment must not be stopped while awaiting confirmatory results.

answers.text: Double the dose of isoniazid and rifampicin at the PHC

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dose escalation of drugs to which the organism is resistant does not overcome resistance. It also adds hepatotoxicity risk without fixing the underlying problem.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Rifampicin resistance on CBNAAT means the standard NTEP regimen will fail, so the patient must be referred immediately to a drug-resistant TB centre for a DR-TB regimen.
Correct. Rifampicin resistance signals DR-TB, which needs a specialised regimen from a DR-TB centre. Directly observed treatment continues during referral.

interactions.label: An ASHA worker does not know that acute flaccid paralysis must be reported immed

params.question: An ASHA worker does not know that acute flaccid paralysis must be reported immediately. What is the most direct consequence for the surveillance system?

answers.text: The reporting chain never starts, so the case never enters the system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Knowledge gaps at the community level stop the chain before it begins. If the ASHA does not recognise the syndrome as reportable, no notification is made and the case stays invisible to surveillance.

answers.text: The case is reported late but accurately on the weekly form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes a timeliness problem. The gap here is more basic: the worker does not recognise the case as reportable at all, so no report is made.

answers.text: The case is entered twice at district level, distorting the counts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Duplicate entries are a data quality problem that arises later in the chain. Here, the case never reaches the system to be duplicated.

answers.text: The patient avoids the health system because of stigma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stigma drives underreporting by discouraging patients from seeking care. It is a different determinant from a worker's knowledge gap, which blocks reporting at the point of recognition.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. A knowledge gap in syndrome recognition stops the reporting chain at its start. The case is never notified, so it never reaches the system at all.

Correct. Knowledge gaps are the most fixable determinant because they block the reporting chain at its origin. A case that is not recognised as reportable never enters the system, however good the later steps are.

interactions.label: A PHC team has built a line list of confirmed cases during an outbreak of gastro

params.question: A PHC team has built a line list of confirmed cases during an outbreak of gastroenteritis. Which step comes next in the standard investigation sequence?

answers.text: Descriptive epidemiology, analysing person, place, and time using the epidemic curve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: After the line list, the team describes who is affected, where cases cluster, and when they occurred. The epidemic curve supports this analysis and generates hypotheses about the source and mode of spread.

answers.text: Case-control or cohort studies to test the source hypothesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Analytic studies test hypotheses. They come after descriptive epidemiology has generated those hypotheses, so this step cannot yet be done.

answers.text: Submission of the final outbreak report to the district authority

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The outbreak report is the last step, communicating findings once control measures and curve evaluation are complete.

answers.text: Evaluation of whether the epidemic curve is declining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Curve evaluation happens after control measures are implemented. Without a hypothesis and control measures in place, there is nothing yet to evaluate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. After the line list, the next step is descriptive epidemiology, where the team analyses who is affected, where cases cluster, and when they occurred. This produces the hypotheses that analytic studies later test.
Correct. Descriptive epidemiology follows the line list. Analysing person, place, and time generates the hypotheses that analytic studies then test.

interactions.label: Which situation requires an ASHA worker to call the PHC medical officer immediat

params.question: Which situation requires an ASHA worker to call the PHC medical officer immediately rather than waiting for the weekly S-form?

answers.text: A child under fifteen with sudden weakness in one leg, suggesting acute flaccid paralysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acute flaccid paralysis is an epidemic-prone syndrome. Its surveillance value depends on rapid notification, so the escalation rule requires an immediate call to the PHC medical officer.

answers.text: A week's tally of uncomplicated fever cases for the routine weekly form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Routine case counts go on the weekly S-form. They do not need immediate escalation unless they form part of a danger-sign pattern.

answers.text: An adult with mild diarrhoea and no vomiting, managed at home with ORS

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mild self-limiting diarrhoea without vomiting does not match the cholera syndrome. It is managed at home and recorded on the routine form.

answers.text: A pregnant woman due for her routine immunization schedule

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Scheduled immunization is a routine service, not an outbreak signal. It is not part of the escalation rule for AFP, cholera, or unexplained deaths.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. The escalation rule covers AFP, cholera, and unexplained deaths. These require an immediate call to the PHC medical officer, because waiting for the weekly S-form could delay the outbreak response.

Correct. AFP, cholera, and unexplained deaths are epidemic-prone syndromes where delay can let transmission or paralysis progress unnoticed, so they are escalated by phone rather than held for the weekly form.
